Chapter 9: The Wisdom of Not-Knowing.
You know, there’s a certain relief in admitting you don’t have all the answers. In a world where everyone seems to prize certainty and expertise, it might feel a little risky to say, “I don’t know.” But, here’s the thing—there’s a real wisdom in not-knowing. There’s a humility that opens the door to learning, to growth, and to genuine connection.
Think about Piglet for a moment. With his open-hearted curiosity, he lives this wisdom every single day.
Imagine a teacher who gets a tough question and, instead of pretending, just says, “Let’s find out together.” That simple admission? It creates space for discovery, for shared exploration. It’s not about having all the answers—it’s about being willing to learn, side by side.
Piglet’s never afraid to ask questions, even if they sound a little silly. He listens more than he talks, and when he doesn’t understand, he just says so. That kind of openness makes him approachable. His friends feel safe sharing their own uncertainties, because they know Piglet’s not going to judge them.
There’s this story where the group runs into a puzzling problem. While everyone else argues over who’s right, Piglet quietly asks, “What if we tried something different?” That one question—his willingness to admit he doesn’t know—leads the group to a brand new solution. One they would’ve missed if they’d all just clung to being right.
Most people don’t realize how freeing it is to let go of the need to be right all the time. When someone’s willing to say, “I don’t know,” it invites others in. It sparks collaboration, and it lets everyone grow together. It’s in that space of not-knowing that real wisdom starts to emerge.
Piglet’s example shows us that humility isn’t about putting yourself down. It’s about being open—to new ideas, to other people, and to the possibility that you might not have it all figured out. In a world full of experts, it’s often the humble learner who discovers the deepest truths.
